report.summary: Two Australian stories lead today: Who Gives A Crap confirmed a third-party breach exposed customer names, contact details and spending data, while Home Affairs officials warned the cost of replacing vulnerable legacy government tech will run to billions. Internationally, SonicWall confirmed an actively exploited SSL-VPN MFA bypass, and a SAML signature bypass in Keycloak came to light. AI-assisted hacking infrastructure linked to South Korean bank breaches was also exposed.

items.title: Who Gives A Crap confirms customer data exposed in third party software breach
items.why: An Australian retailer's third-party breach exposed names, contact details and spending figures — useful for targeted phishing — highlighting supplier data-sharing risk.

items.title: The cost of fixing govt’s legacy tech: billions, or far less?
items.why: Home Affairs officials say replacing vulnerable legacy systems across federal government will cost billions, a major planning and budget challenge for national cyber defences.

items.title: OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass on Alpine Linux (*sshole) – CVE-2026-123158
items.why: CVE-2026-123158 lets long passwords bypass authentication on Alpine Linux OpenSSH, potentially reaching root on cloud systems; patches are out.

items.title: CVE-2026-19868: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability
items.why: This SonicWall SSLVPN flaw (CVE-2026-19868) can bypass SAML-enforced MFA and is on CISA's known-exploited list, so edge-device MFA alone can't be relied on.

items.title: Keycloak CVE-2026-117691: How a SAML Signature Bypass Skips Authentication
items.why: A SAML signature bypass in Keycloak (CVE-2026-117691) could let attackers authenticate as other users, though exploitation status and affected versions are unconfirmed.
